title: Working-class identity is broader than income or blue-collar work and increasingly carries partisan meaning
source_unit: Pew Research Center data essay, Who Sees Themselves as Working Class?, August 31, 2026
geography: United States; adults nationally with income, education, race/ethnicity, occupation, financial-stress, and party comparisons

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew American Trends Panel survey

working_class_total.unit: percent saying working class describes them extremely or very well; 54% in 2024

college_graduate.unit: percent of adults with a bachelor's degree or more

no_college_degree.unit: percent of adults without a bachelor's degree

party_gap.value: 67% Republican or Republican-leaning versus 55% Democratic or Democratic-leaning

observations.method: Pew survey of 8,512 U.S. adults conducted January 20-26, 2026; the working-class question asks whether the term describes the respondent extremely or very well.
observations.uncertainty: Self-identification is not a direct measure of income, wealth, occupation, class position, or material hardship; the increase from 2024 is descriptive and does not identify a cause.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by education, adjusted family-income tier, and partisan identification.
observations.counterinterpretation: The term may function as a moral, cultural, or political identity as much as an economic category, so broad adoption does not mean economic conditions are converging.

observations.period: January 2026; identity versus financial security and occupation

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the January 2026 Pew survey; linked subgroup measures use their relevant weighted universes

financially_comfortable_working_class.unit: percent of adults who consistently pay bills in full, have several months of emergency savings, and meet expenses comfortably

other_workers_working_class.unit: percent of workers in other occupations

observations.method: January 2026 identity data linked to a November 2025 financial-stress scale and October 2024 occupation data; Pew defines blue-collar workers using physical labor and specified industrial sectors.
observations.uncertainty: The linked surveys are not a same-day causal design, and the blue-collar definition excludes some workers who may understand themselves as working class; financial comfort is self-reported.
observations.subgroup: Adults by financial-stress level and workers by blue-collar versus other occupation type.
observations.counterinterpretation: Material security and occupational position still matter, but the overlap shows that working-class language can describe dignity, dependence on work, social origin, or political belonging beyond current hardship.

observations.period: January 2026; partisan meaning across economic categories

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Pew survey; party and subgroup estimates use weighted subgroup universes

upper_income_party_gap.value: 61% Republican or Republican-leaning versus 38% Democratic or Democratic-leaning
upper_income_party_gap.unit: upper-income adults identifying as working class

low_financial_stress_party_gap.value: 60% Republican or Republican-leaning versus 39% Democratic or Democratic-leaning
low_financial_stress_party_gap.unit: low-financial-stress adults identifying as working class

blue_collar_party_gap.value: 82% Republican or Republican-leaning versus 72% Democratic or Democratic-leaning
blue_collar_party_gap.unit: blue-collar workers identifying as working class

other_worker_party_gap.value: 68% Republican or Republican-leaning versus 55% Democratic or Democratic-leaning
other_worker_party_gap.unit: workers in other occupations identifying as working class

observations.method: Pew cross-tabulation and multivariate analysis relating working-class identification to party, income, financial stress, education, race/ethnicity, age, gender, and occupation.
observations.uncertainty: These are associations, not evidence that party identity causes class identification; subgroup estimates can reflect different histories, narratives, or interpretations of the term.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults across income, financial-stress, education, and occupational groups, split by party.
observations.counterinterpretation: The partisan pattern may be a contest over who gets to represent work and ordinary life, rather than a stable economic coalition; policy preferences are not measured by the identity question alone.

observations.period: January 2026; race, education, and class language

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Pew survey; race and education estimates use weighted subgroup universes

white_total.unit: percent of White adults identifying as working class

asian_total.unit: percent of Asian adults; English-speaker estimate

white_education_gap.value: 71% without a college degree versus 48% with a degree
white_education_gap.unit: White adults identifying as working class

hispanic_black_education_pattern.value: 61% of Hispanic and 58% of Black college graduates identify as working class

observations.method: Pew racial and ethnic comparisons use the January 2026 survey; White, Black, and Asian adults are non-Hispanic single-race respondents and Hispanics may be of any race.
observations.uncertainty: Some subgroup samples are small, including Black and Asian Republicans; racial and educational differences do not reveal which meanings respondents attach to the term.
observations.subgroup: White, Hispanic, Black, and Asian adults by education and party.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different group patterns suggest that class language is culturally situated and cannot be interpreted as a single national hierarchy or universal economic self-description.

boundary: This record treats working-class identity as a cultural and political classification layer connecting work, status, financial security, race, and party. It does not define the American working class, establish economic mobility, infer policy preferences, or turn self-identification into a respondent-level causal explanation.
